description:
A function body made of N statements of the form `if n == i, do: f(n)` makes one activation analysis take about 2x longer per added statement.

## Reproduce

    def f(x), do: [x]
    def main() do
      n = length(System.argv()) + 100
      if n == 0, do: f(n)
      if n == 1, do: f(n)
      ...            # N statements
      :ok
    end

`fz2 interp` at develop 4f8b72ea4 (debug build, opt-level 1):

| N  | wall   | jobs |
|----|--------|------|
| 8  | 0.12 s | 852  |
| 10 | 0.12 s | 852  |
| 12 | 0.32 s | 852  |
| 14 | 1.64 s | 852  |
| 16 | 5.90 s | 852  |

An earlier measurement had 20 statements at 40 s. It reproduced before the exceptions work landed, so it is not caused by it.

## What is known

- The job count does not move with N. The time is inside single jobs: in the N=16 trace the longest spans are all `AnalyzeActivation` of `main` (function_id 1, arrow 15), about 0.6 to 0.9 s each, run several times.
- So the growth is in the body walk of one activation, not in scheduling.

## What is not known

Which part of the walk doubles. Candidates to separate by experiment: each `if` without `else` joining two environments that are then both carried forward (2^N paths), or the narrowing of `n` by each `n == i` test producing a type whose size doubles.

## Done when

The table above is linear in N, with a test that pins the cost of one activation analysis against N.
title: Analysing a function with N sequential if statements costs about twice as much per added statement
